claim: WASP deficiency results in defects in calcium ion signaling, cytoskeletal regulation, gene transcription and overall T cell activation.
source: Wiscott Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASP) deficiency results in defects in calcium ion signaling, cytoskeletal regulation, gene transcription and overall T cell activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these defects in WASP-deficient cells.

claim: When WASP function is eliminated there is negligible effect on actin polymerization at the immunological synapse.
source: Yet, when WASP function is eliminated there is negligible effect on actin polymerization at the immunological synapse, leading to gaps in our understanding of the events connecting WASP and calcium ion signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about prior observations in the field that motivated the current study.

claim: WASP generates a fraction of total synaptic F-actin selectively in the form of distinct F-actin 'foci'.
source: Here, we identify a fraction of total synaptic F-actin selectively generated by WASP in the form of distinct F-actin 'foci'.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: F-actin foci are polymerized de novo as a result of the T cell receptor (TCR) proximal tyrosine kinase cascade.
source: These foci are polymerized de novo as a result of the T cell receptor (TCR) proximal tyrosine kinase cascade, and facilitate distal signaling events including PLCγ1 activation and subsequent cytoplasmic calcium ion elevation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: F-actin foci facilitate distal signaling events including PLCγ1 activation and subsequent cytoplasmic calcium ion elevation.
source: These foci are polymerized de novo as a result of the T cell receptor (TCR) proximal tyrosine kinase cascade, and facilitate distal signaling events including PLCγ1 activation and subsequent cytoplasmic calcium ion elevation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 4, 5, and 6.

claim: WASP generates a dynamic F-actin architecture in the context of the immunological synapse, which then amplifies the downstream signals required for an optimal immune response.
source: We conclude that WASP generates a dynamic F-actin architecture in the context of the immunological synapse, which then amplifies the downstream signals required for an optimal immune response.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: TCR signaling is initiated at F-actin-based protrusions of polarized T cells.
source: First, TCR signaling is initiated at F-actin-based protrusions of polarized T cells (Valitutti et al., 1995; Negulescu et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Early activation events lead to F-actin dependent formation of a broad immunological synapse (IS).
source: Next, these early activation events lead to F-actin dependent formation of a broad immunological synapse (IS) (Wülfing and Davis, 1998; Grakoui et al., 1999) containing T cell antigen receptor (TCR) microclusters (MCs) (Bunnell et al., 2002; Campi et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The immunological synapse contains T cell antigen receptor (TCR) microclusters (MCs).
source: Next, these early activation events lead to F-actin dependent formation of a broad immunological synapse (IS) (Wülfing and Davis, 1998; Grakoui et al., 1999) containing T cell antigen receptor (TCR) microclusters (MCs) (Bunnell et al., 2002; Campi et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Synapse spreading is followed by myosin II dependent contraction to form supramolecular activation clusters (SMACs).
source: Synapse spreading is followed by myosin II dependent contraction to form supramolecular activation clusters (SMACs) (Monks et al., 1998; Griffiths et al., 2001; Ilani et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TCR MCs form in the outer lamellipodia-like 'distal' (d)SMAC.
source: TCR MCs form in the outer lamellipodia-like 'distal' (d)SMAC, after which signaling MCs move centripetally through the lamella like 'peripheral' (p)SMAC, driven by centripetal flow of F-actin (Ponti et al., 2004; Varma et al., 2006; DeMond et al., 2008; Vardhana et al., 2010; Kumari et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012) to eventually reach the 'central' (c)SMAC.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Signaling MCs move centripetally through the lamella like 'peripheral' (p)SMAC, driven by centripetal flow of F-actin.
source: TCR MCs form in the outer lamellipodia-like 'distal' (d)SMAC, after which signaling MCs move centripetally through the lamella like 'peripheral' (p)SMAC, driven by centripetal flow of F-actin (Ponti et al., 2004; Varma et al., 2006; DeMond et al., 2008; Vardhana et al., 2010; Kumari et al., 2012; Yi et al., 2012) to eventually reach the 'central' (c)SMAC.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cSMAC is an F-actin depleted zone.
source: The cSMAC is an F-actin depleted zone (Stinchcombe et al., 2006), in which TCR is destined for down-regulation via extracellular vesicle formation (Vardhana et al., 2010; Choudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the cSMAC, TCR is destined for down-regulation via extracellular vesicle formation.
source: The cSMAC is an F-actin depleted zone (Stinchcombe et al., 2006), in which TCR is destined for down-regulation via extracellular vesicle formation (Vardhana et al., 2010; Choudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of global F-actin or genetic manipulations that reduce synaptic F-actin polymerization result in defects in early signaling events such as cell adhesion, TCR MC formation, early TCR signaling, TCR MC transport, as well as the TCR-distal events including intracellular calcium rise, and store operated calcium ion entry.
source: Pharmacological disruption of global F-actin or genetic manipulations that reduce synaptic F-actin polymerization result in defects in early signaling events such as cell adhesion, TCR MC formation, early TCR signaling, TCR MC transport, as well as the TCR-distal events including intracellular calcium rise, and store operated calcium ion entry (DeBell et al., 1992; Valitutti et al., 1995; Campi et al., 2005; Nolz et al., 2006; Varma et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: WAS T cells exhibit a variety of T cell activation defects such as aberrant synapse morphology, impaired proliferation in response to TCR-activation stimuli, and impaired calcium ion signaling.
source: WAS T cells exhibit a variety of T cell activation defects such as aberrant synapse morphology, impaired proliferation in response to TCR-activation stimuli, and impaired calcium ion signaling (Molina et al., 1993; Cianferoni et al., 2005; Calvez et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: T cells from Was−/− mice display profound defects in antigen receptor-induced proliferation, IS stability, nuclear NFAT translocation and IL-2 production.
source: Similar to WAS patients, T cells from Was−/− mice also display profound defects in antigen receptor-induced proliferation, IS stability, nuclear NFAT translocation and IL-2 production (Snapper et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1999, 2002; Cannon and Burkhardt, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: T cells from Was−/− mice and human WAS T cells have apparently normal total F-actin levels as well as SMAC organization within the immunological synapse.
source: T cells from Was−/− mice (Zhang et al., 1999; Krawczyk et al., 2002; Cannon and Burkhardt, 2004; Sims et al., 2007) and human WAS T cells (Molina et al., 1993; Dupre et al., 2002; Calvez et al., 2011) have apparently normal total F-actin levels as well as SMAC organization within the immunological synapse, while initial TCR–associated kinase signaling in response to MHC-peptide complexes in the context of adhesion ligands is also intact (Rengan et al., 2000; Sato et al., 2001; Krawczyk et al., 2002; Cannon and Burkhardt, 2004; Sims et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Initial TCR–associated kinase signaling in response to MHC-peptide complexes in the context of adhesion ligands is intact in T cells from Was−/− mice and human WAS T cells.
source: T cells from Was−/− mice (Zhang et al., 1999; Krawczyk et al., 2002; Cannon and Burkhardt, 2004; Sims et al., 2007) and human WAS T cells (Molina et al., 1993; Dupre et al., 2002; Calvez et al., 2011) have apparently normal total F-actin levels as well as SMAC organization within the immunological synapse, while initial TCR–associated kinase signaling in response to MHC-peptide complexes in the context of adhesion ligands is also intact (Rengan et al., 2000; Sato et al., 2001; Krawczyk et al., 2002; Cannon and Burkhardt, 2004; Sims et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HS1 deficient T cells show defects similar to WASP−/− T cells in TCR activation dependent calcium elevation, proliferation, IL-2 secretion and NFAT activation.
source: HS1 deficient T cells show defects similar to WASP−/− T cells in TCR activation dependent calcium elevation, proliferation, IL-2 secretion and NFAT activation (Taniuchi et al., 1995; Hutchcroft et al., 1998; Gomez et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TCR ligation triggers a molecular program that results in activation of phospholipase C-γ1 (PLCγ1), through phosphorylation on Y-783 by Itk.
source: TCR ligation triggers a molecular program that results in activation of phospholipase C-γ1 (PLCγ1), through phosphorylation on Y-783 by Itk (Park et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Once activated, phospho-PLCγ1 catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidylinositol-4,5 bisphosphate (PIP2) to inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol.
source: Once it has been activated, phospho-PLCγ1 catalyzes the conversion of phosphatidylinositol-4,5 bisphosphate (PIP2) to inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about PLCγ1 function.

claim: IP3 acts as a second messenger and facilitates release of calcium ions from intracellular stores.
source: IP3 then acts as a second messenger and facilitates release of calcium ions from intracellular stores.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about IP3 function.

claim: Following TCR activation, PLCγ1 recruitment at the synapse is primarily mediated via binding to linker of activated T cells (LAT).
source: Following TCR activation, PLCγ1 recruitment at the synapse is primarily mediated via binding to linker of activated T cells (LAT) (Braiman et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: WT T cells exhibited discrete F-actin rich features referred to as F-actin 'foci'.
source: WT T cells exhibited discrete F-actin rich features (Figure 1A, arrowheads). We refer to these structures as F-actin 'foci'.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: F-actin foci incorporate fresh actin subunits, indicating that the foci are dynamically polymerizing structures.
source: Assessment of the amount of newly polymerized actin in foci vs surrounding lamellar areas using the above-mentioned labeling and quantification method revealed that the F-actin foci incorporate fresh actin subunits (Figure 1B). This indicates that the foci are dynamically polymerizing structures, rather than sites where F-actin accumulates due to rearrangement of preexisting filaments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by barbed-end labeling experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The polymerization rate of individual filaments (Fresh/Total ratio) is similar between foci and surrounding areas in WT T cells.
source: Furthermore, the polymerization rate of individual filaments (Fresh/Total ratio) is similar between foci and surrounding areas in WT T cells (Figure 1B), indicating that the foci result from preferential local nucleation, rather than enhanced polymerization rate of existing filaments.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of barbed-end labeling data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Overall synaptic F-actin levels, as well as the rate of actin polymerization were similar in WT and WASP−/− T cells.
source: When compared at the whole synapse scale, overall synaptic F-actin levels, as well as the rate of actin polymerization were similar in WT and WASP−/− T cells, as expected (Cannon and Burkhardt, 2004).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by data in Figure 1C and consistent with prior literature.

claim: There was a significant reduction in F-actin foci in WASP−/− cell synapse.
source: However, there was a significant reduction in F-actin foci in WASP−/− cell synapse (Figure 1C), suggesting that dynamic F-actin foci are formed in a WASP dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Acute siRNA mediated knockdown of WASP in activated mouse CD4 T cells resulted in a similar phenotype to the WASP−/− T cells with no reduction in total F-actin and significant reductions in foci.
source: The loss of foci in WASP−/− T cells is not due to non-specific developmental defects, since acute siRNA mediated knockdown of WASP in activated mouse CD4 T cells resulted in a similar phenotype to the WASP−/− T cells. No reduction in total F-actin and significant reductions in foci were observed in WASP siRNA transfected cells imaged on SLB with anti-CD3 and ICAM1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Primary CD4 T cells from Wasl−/− mice formed immunological synapses with F-actin foci similar to T cells from WT mice.
source: However, primary CD4 T cells from Wasl−/− mice (Figure 1D) formed immunological synapses with F-actin foci similar to T cells from WT mice.
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Activation of T cells with anti-CD3 and ICAM1 recruited NWASP and WAVE2 to the IS.
source: Instead, we determined the localization of NWASP and WAVE2 in the immunological synapse in order to gain further insight into their possible role in foci formation. Activation of T cells with anti-CD3 and ICAM1 recruited NWASP and WAVE2 to the IS (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) (Nolz et al., 2006), but the recruited proteins failed to co-localize with F-actin foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, NWASP coloc. = 9.48% ± 0.76 n = 78; WAVE2 coloc. = 14.36% ± 1.25, n = 54).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: NWASP and WAVE2 failed to co-localize with F-actin foci.
source: Activation of T cells with anti-CD3 and ICAM1 recruited NWASP and WAVE2 to the IS (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A) (Nolz et al., 2006), but the recruited proteins failed to co-localize with F-actin foci (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B, NWASP coloc. = 9.48% ± 0.76 n = 78; WAVE2 coloc. = 14.36% ± 1.25, n = 54).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by colocalization analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: F-actin foci formation was only marginally impaired in HS1−/− T cells, this reduction was modest compared to T cells from mice lacking both HS1 and WASP.
source: F-actin foci formation was only marginally impaired in HS1−/− T cells, this reduction was modest compared to T cells from mice lacking both HS1 and WASP (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A similar marginal reduction in F-actin foci intensity was obtained by siRNA-mediated knockdown of HS1 in activated mouse CD4 T cells.
source: A similar marginal reduction in F-actin foci intensity was obtained by siRNA-mediated knockdown of HS1 in activated mouse CD4 T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: WT mouse CD4 T cells activated with anti-CD3 and ICAM1 displayed foci of phospho-HS1 in the synapse.
source: We next determined if this phosphorylation is WASP dependent. WT mouse CD4 T cells activated with anti-CD3 and ICAM1 displayed foci of phospho-HS1 in the synapse (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Phospho-HS1 foci were significantly reduced in WASP−/− or WASP−/− NWASP−/− CD4 T cells, but not in CD4 T cells from NWASP deficient mice.
source: These phospho-HS1 foci were significantly reduced in WASP−/− or WASP−/− NWASP−/− CD4 T cells, but not in CD4 T cells from NWASP deficient mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: In murine polyclonal CD4 T cells activated on anti-CD3 and ICAM1 containing bilayers, TCR MC localized with F-actin foci.
source: In murine polyclonal CD4 T cells activated on anti-CD3 and ICAM1 containing bilayers, as in Figure 1, TCR MC localized with F-actin foci (Figure 2A, upper panels, arrows).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Similar co-localization of F-actin foci with TCR MC was observed with monoclonal AND TCR transgenic T cells stimulated with MHCp and ICAM1.
source: Similar co-localization of F-actin foci with TCR MC was observed with monoclonal AND TCR transgenic T cells stimulated with MHCp and ICAM1 (Figure 2A, lower panels).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: After 1 min of cell attachment, 40 ± 1.7% of TCR MCs co-localized with F-actin foci in AND T cells.
source: After 1 min of cell attachment, 40 ± 1.7% of TCR MCs co-localized with F-actin foci in these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, 'Materials and methods', Figure 2B), significantly above chance level co-localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), whereas only 15 ± 0.07% of total ICAM1 exhibited association with actin foci (Figure 2B), which was not different from chance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only 15 ± 0.07% of total ICAM1 exhibited association with actin foci, which was not different from chance.
source: After 1 min of cell attachment, 40 ± 1.7% of TCR MCs co-localized with F-actin foci in these cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, 'Materials and methods', Figure 2B), significantly above chance level co-localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), whereas only 15 ± 0.07% of total ICAM1 exhibited association with actin foci (Figure 2B), which was not different from chance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: F-actin foci formed in WASP-dependent manner in Human primary CD4 T cells.
source: When examined in Human primary CD4 T cells as well, F-actin foci formed in WASP-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and TCR MCs, but not ICAM1 MCs, were associated with F-actin foci (TCR co-localization with F-actin foci was 34.5% ± 2.0, n = 76, co-localization of ICAM1 with F-actin foci was 13.1% ± 0.8, n = 66) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In human primary CD4 T cells, TCR MCs, but not ICAM1 MCs, were associated with F-actin foci (TCR co-localization with F-actin foci was 34.5% ± 2.0, n = 76, co-localization of ICAM1 with F-actin foci was 13.1% ± 0.8, n = 66).
source: When examined in Human primary CD4 T cells as well, F-actin foci formed in WASP-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B), and TCR MCs, but not ICAM1 MCs, were associated with F-actin foci (TCR co-localization with F-actin foci was 34.5% ± 2.0, n = 76, co-localization of ICAM1 with F-actin foci was 13.1% ± 0.8, n = 66) (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of colocalization analysis shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: TCR-activation led to HS1 phosphorylation at the T cell synapse.
source: Furthermore, TCR-activation led to HS1 phosphorylation at the T cell synapse, as shown previously (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) (Hutchcroft et al., 1998; Gomez et al., 2006), and the phospho-HS1 co-localized with F-actin foci in both TCR-activation stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Phospho-HS1 co-localized with F-actin foci in both TCR-activation stimuli.
source: Furthermore, TCR-activation led to HS1 phosphorylation at the T cell synapse, as shown previously (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A) (Hutchcroft et al., 1998; Gomez et al., 2006), and the phospho-HS1 co-localized with F-actin foci in both TCR-activation stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The F-actin signal progressively decreases toward the synapse center where central TCR MC are devoid of F-actin foci.
source: As expected (Stinchcombe et al., 2006), the F-actin signal progressively decreases toward the synapse center where central TCR MC are devoid of F-actin foci (Figure 2—figure supplement 4, asterisks in the 'Merge' panel).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and consistent with prior literature.

claim: In live cell synapses, LifeAct-GFP was observed to form foci on TCR MCs, which continued to co-migrate until the delivery of MCs to the cSMAC.
source: In live cell synapses, LifeAct-GFP was observed to form foci on TCR MCs, which continued to co-migrate until the delivery of MCs to the cSMAC (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Video 3).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and Video 3.

claim: The average TCR MC speed was 5.66 ± 2.2 μm/min, average Foci speed was 6.63 ± 3.1 μm/min (p = 0.21, ns).
source: Analysis of kymographs revealed that the average TCR MC speed was 5.66 ± 2.2 μm/min, average Foci speed was 6.63 ± 3.1 μm/min (p = 0.21, ns).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of live cell imaging data.

claim: The TCR signals persisted in the cSMAC, whereas the GFP foci were extinguished.
source: The TCR signals persisted in the cSMAC, whereas the GFP foci were extinguished, consistent with continual nucleation of F-actin at the MC site (Figure 1A) until it reaches the cSMAC, where TCR signals are known to be terminated (Vardhana et al., 2010; Choudhuri et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live cell imaging data and consistent with prior literature.

claim: The Jurkat T cell line stimulated using a similar anti-CD3 and ICAM1 activation system displayed only random co-localization of TCR MC and F-actin (9.0% ± 0.09 TCR colocalized with F-actin, n = 47).
source: We also note that the Jurkat T cell line stimulated using a similar anti-CD3 and ICAM1 activation system displayed only random co-localization of TCR MC and F-actin (9.0% ± 0.09 TCR colocalized with F-actin, n = 47, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, right panels, Video 4).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A significant induction of F-actin foci only occurred when AND TCR transgenic T cells were incubated with both ICAM1 and agonist peptide-MHC.
source: AND T cells activated using ICAM1 alone displayed some interface F-actin (Figure 3A, top images); however, a significant induction of F-actin foci only occurred when AND TCR transgenic T cells were incubated with both ICAM1 and agonist peptide-MHC (Figure 3A, top graph).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A similar requirement of TCR triggering for F-actin foci formation was observed in primary human CD4 T cells.
source: A similar requirement of TCR triggering for F-actin foci formation was observed in primary human CD4 T cells (Figure 3A, bottom graph), although it did not scale with the dose of TCR agonist; in T cells incubated with low or high concentrations of anti-CD3 antibody, we did not observe a corresponding increase in F-actin foci (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phospho-SFK localized to F-actin foci associated MC.
source: TCR signaling proceeds by accumulation of active Lck, as indicated by phosphorylation of the activation loop, in MCs (Campi et al., 2005). Consistent with this, phospho-SFK localized to F-actin foci associated MC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of SFK phosphorylation using PP2 significantly reduced the number of F-actin foci.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of SFK phosphorylation using PP2 (Varma et al., 2006) significantly reduced the number of F-actin foci (Figure 3B), indicating that TCR-driven SFK signaling is required for their formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: TCR-induced Zap70 Y319 phosphorylation in MC and overall F-actin levels at the synapse were comparable between primary WT and WASP−/− cells.
source: TCR-induced Zap70 Y319 phosphorylation in MC and overall F-actin levels at the synapse were comparable between primary WT and WASP−/− cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: WASP−/− T cells exhibited significantly reduced phospho-PLCγ1 levels at the synapse.
source: WASP−/− T cells exhibited significantly reduced phospho-PLCγ1 levels at the synapse (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The reduction in phospho-PLCγ1 levels was not due to a general decrease in total PLCγ1 levels in the WASP−/− T cells, as the levels of total cellular PLCγ1 were comparable in WT and WASP−/− whole T cell lysates.
source: The reduction in phospho-PLCγ1 levels was not due to a general decrease in total PLCγ1 levels in the WASP−/− T cells, as the levels of total cellular PLCγ1 were comparable in WT and WASP−/− whole T cell lysates (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: T cells expressing GFP-WASPΔC showed normal levels of Arp2/3 complex recruitment, as well as total F-actin at the synapse, and synaptic recruitment of WASPΔC was comparable to WT WASP.
source: Indeed, T cells expressing GFP-WASPΔC showed normal levels of Arp2/3 complex recruitment (data not shown), as well as total F-actin at the synapse, and synaptic recruitment of WASPΔC was comparable to WT WASP (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: WASPΔC expressing cells were severely defective in F-actin foci generation, as well as in PLCγ1 phosphorylation at the synapse.
source: However, WASPΔC expressing cells were severely defective in F-actin foci generation, as well as in PLCγ1 phosphorylation at the synapse (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Overexpression of WASP Y291F had no effect on foci formation or PLCγ1 activation.
source: Overexpression of WASP Y291F (Dovas et al., 2009), a mutant form defective in phosphorylation dependent interaction with SH2 domain of SFKs (Padrick and Rosen, 2010), had no effect on foci formation or PLCγ1 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A significant fraction of endogenous Arp2/3 complex is recruited at the TCR MC sites.
source: A significant fraction of endogenous Arp2/3 complex is recruited at the TCR MC sites (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In T cells treated with CK666, the association of both Arpc2 and 3 with TCR MCs was reduced.
source: In T cells treated with CK666, a small molecule inhibitor affecting conformational change in Arp2/3 complex and thus actin nucleation (Nolen et al., 2009), the association of both Arpc2 and 3 with TCR MCs was reduced (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CK666 treatment led to loss of F-actin foci.
source: The same treatment conditions also led to loss of F-actin foci (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: CK689, an inactive isomer of CK666, and the inhibitor for another class of actin nucleation factors, formins, or inhibition of myosin II using blebbistatin did not inhibit F-actin foci.
source: As a control, CK689, an inactive isomer of CK666 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and the inhibitor for another class of actin nucleation factors, formins (Rizvi et al., 2009), or inhibition of myosin II using blebbistatin (Straight et al., 2003), did not inhibit F-actin foci (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), indicating that these foci specifically require Arp2/3 complex for nucleation, and myosin-mediated actin rearrangement is not required for their formation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Incubation with the patterned surface triggered rapid actin polymerization at the anti-CD3 microdot, reflected in LifeAct-GFP accumulation.
source: Incubation with the patterned surface triggered rapid actin polymerization at the anti-CD3 microdot, reflected in LifeAct-GFP accumulation (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 5C–E.

claim: Within 5 s of CK666 treatment, pre-existing LifeAct enrichment was lost from the microdot site.
source: Within 5 s of CK666 treatment, pre-existing LifeAct enrichment was lost from the microdot site (Figure 5C–E Video 5) and fresh microdot contact events failed to elicit LifeAct-GFP enrichment in the presence of CK666 (Video 5).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 5C–E and Video 5.

claim: CK666 treatment, which resulted in severe inhibition of F-actin foci, did not diminish TCR-proximal activation events.
source: CK666 treatment, which resulted in severe inhibition of F-actin foci (Figure 5B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), did not diminish TCR-proximal activation events.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: F-actin dependent processes including formation of TCR MC and exclusion of CD45 phosphatase from MCs proceeded normally in CK666-treated cells.
source: While fewer T cells formed synapses after CK666 treatment (37% reduction), upon adhesion, F-actin dependent processes including formation of TCR MC and exclusion of CD45 phosphatase from MCs (Campi et al., 2005; Varma et al., 2006) (Figure 6A), and the phosphorylation of Zap70 on Y319 (Figure 6B) proceeded normally in CK666-treated cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The phosphorylation of Zap70 on Y319 proceeded normally in CK666-treated cells.
source: While fewer T cells formed synapses after CK666 treatment (37% reduction), upon adhesion, F-actin dependent processes including formation of TCR MC and exclusion of CD45 phosphatase from MCs (Campi et al., 2005; Varma et al., 2006) (Figure 6A), and the phosphorylation of Zap70 on Y319 (Figure 6B) proceeded normally in CK666-treated cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A severe defect was observed in the levels of TCR-induced PLCγ1 phosphorylation on Y783 after CK666 treatment.
source: However, a severe defect was observed in the levels of TCR-induced PLCγ1 phosphorylation on Y783 after CK666 treatment (Figure 6C,D), where a drop was observed in both the number and intensity of phospho-PLCγ1 clusters at the synapse (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: While phospho-PLCγ1 localized with F-actin foci in control cells, treatment with CK666 led to loss of foci-associated phospho-PLCγ1.
source: Furthermore, while phospho-PLCγ1 localized with F-actin foci in control cells, treatment with CK666 led to loss of foci-associated phospho-PLCγ1 (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by colocalization analysis of microscopy data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Upon attenuation of F-actin foci, total PLCγ1 levels were also reduced at the synapse, matching the decline in phospho-PLCγ1 levels.
source: Upon attenuation of F-actin foci, total PLCγ1 levels were also reduced at the synapse, matching the decline in phospho-PLCγ1 levels (Figure 6F) and indicating that the impaired levels of phospho-PLCγ1 at the whole cell level may be accounted for by the reduction in PLCγ1 enrichment at the TCR signalosome.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: CK666-treated cells showed significant reduction in TCR-induced calcium ion elevation in the cytoplasm and nuclear mobilization of NFAT1.
source: When assaying signaling events downstream of PLCγ1 activation, such as TCR-induced calcium ion elevation in the cytoplasm and nuclear mobilization of NFAT1, CK666-treated cells showed significant reduction in these processes (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of calcium imaging and microscopy data shown in Figure 6G,H.

claim: CK666 treatment of cells led to a reduction of PLCγ1 enrichment at microdots.
source: Human CD4 T cells expressing PLCγ1-YFP were incubated with micron-size immobile anti-CD3 dots, and visualized using live cell imaging immediately after cell attachment. Similar to F-actin foci assembly at the microdot, PLCγ1 enrichment was also visible at the microdot sites. CK666 treatment of cells led to a reduction of PLCγ1 enrichment at microdots (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of live cell imaging data shown in Figure 6I,J.

claim: ILPs were associated with the Y397 phosphorylated form of HS1, similar to F-actin foci.
source: Using this system, F-actin and HS1 rich 'invadopod-like-protrusions' (ILPs) are observed at TCR MC-like features in the periphery of the synapse (Sage et al., 2012). We found that ILPs were associated with the Y397 phosphorylated form of HS1, similar to F-actin foci (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a primary observation supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When pre-formed T cell-EC conjugates were treated with CK666, there was concomitant loss of ILPs and phospho-HS1.
source: Furthermore, when pre-formed T cell-EC conjugates were treated with CK666, there was concomitant loss of ILPs and phospho-HS1, indicating that these structures also require Arp2/3-dependent continuous polymerization of F-actin, and support local phospho-HS1 levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: WASP silenced T cells display selective loss of both ILPs as well as phospho-HS1, while maintaining total F-actin levels.
source: WASP silenced T cells display selective loss of both ILPs as well as phospho-HS1, while maintaining total F-actin levels (Figure 7A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification of microscopy data shown in Figure 7A–C.
